text: The Taipei 101 (Chinese: 台北101; pinyin: Táiběi 101; stylized in all caps), formerly known as the Taipei World Financial Center, is a 508 m (1,667 ft), 101-story skyscraper located in Taipei, Taiwan, owned by the Taipei Financial Center Corporation. It was officially recognized as the world's tallest building from its opening on 31 December 2004 until it was surpassed by the Burj Khalifa in 2009. Upon completion, it became the world's first skyscraper to exceed half a kilometer and remains the tallest building in Taiwan and the eleventh tallest in the world according to the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat's official rankings. The building's high-speed elevators, manufactured by Toshiba of Japan, held the world record for speed at the time of completion, transporting passengers from the 5th to the 89th floor in 37 seconds (attaining 60.6 km/h or 37.7 mph). In 2011, Taipei 101 received a Platinum certification under the LEED certification system for energy efficiency and environmental design, becoming the tallest and largest green building in the world. The structure regularly appears as an icon of Taipei in international media, with Taipei 101 fireworks displays being a regular feature of New Year's Eve broadcasts and celebrations. Its postmodernist architectural style incorporates traditional Asian aesthetics using industrial materials and is designed to withstand earthquakes and tropical storms common in the region. The tower features a large wind damper, the largest in the world, measuring 18 feet across, and a 660-metric-ton steel pendulum suspended between the 88th and 92nd floors, which reduces up to 40% of the building's movements and was recorded at a 1-meter sway during Typhoon Soudelor in 2015. The damper, composed of 41 circular steel plates welded into a 5.5-meter-diameter ball, has become a popular tourist attraction, leading to the creation of a mascot named Damper Baby by Sanrio. The building's blue-green glass curtain walls are double-pane and block 50% of external heat and UV radiation, and can withstand impacts of 7 metric tons. The facade features a "double stairstep" corner design to reduce crosswind oscillations, and includes symbolic elements such as the ruyi, which appears throughout the structure and on the mall's roof, with each ruyi at least 8 meters tall. The number 101 commemorates the start of a new century (100+1) and the renewal of time, symbolizing perfection and digital technology, while the eight segments of eight floors each reflect the number eight, associated with prosperity and good fortune in Chinese culture. The design also evokes the rhythms of an Asian pagoda, a stalk of bamboo, and ancient Chinese money boxes. The building's foundation consists of 380 piles driven 80 meters into the ground, extending 30 meters into bedrock, each 1.5 meters in diameter and capable of bearing 1,000–1,320 metric tons. Planning began in July 1997 during Chen Shui-bian's term as Taipei mayor, with initial proposals for a 66-story tower, later expanded to 101 stories after an expat suggested the increased height and other design features. The city granted a construction license for a 101-story tower in the summer of 2000, and the first tower column was erected in 2001. A major earthquake on 31 March 2002 caused a crane to fall from the 56th floor, resulting in five deaths, but no structural damage was found, and construction resumed within a week. The roof was completed on 1 July 2003, and the building was completed in 2004, with construction led by a joint venture between Kumagai Gumi (Japan) and Samsung C&T (South Korea), where Samsung C&T oversaw the main structural framework and RESE managed logistics and foundation. Ma Ying-jeou fastened a golden bolt to mark the completion, and the formal opening occurred on 31 December 2004, with President Chen Shui-bian, Taipei Mayor Ma Ying-jeou, and Legislative Speaker Wang Jin-pyng cutting the ribbon, followed by open-air concerts featuring A-Mei and Stefanie Sun and the first fireworks show. Taipei 101 displaced the Petronas Towers as the world's tallest building by 57.3 meters (188 feet), with its roof height at 449.2 meters (1,474 feet) and highest occupied floor at 439.2 meters (1,441 feet), surpassing the previous records of the Willis Tower and the Tuntex Sky Tower in Kaohsiung. The building's roof and facade recycled water system meets 20–30% of its water needs. In 2019, it was named among the 50 most influential skyscrapers in the world. On 4 January 2020, it displayed a condolence message in lights for victims of a helicopter crash, and on 8 February 2020, it was reported that some passengers from the Diamond Princess cruise ship, quarantined for a COVID-19 outbreak, had visited the building on 31 January without symptoms. On 1 April 2020, the shopping center reduced business hours due to the pandemic, began checking shopper temperatures in February, and resumed normal operations in June 2020. The building hosts various events, including art exhibits in the Observatory, and the New Year's Eve fireworks display is held at Taipei City Hall, with crowds also gathering at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall. The height of the building is measured from the top of a 1.2-meter platform at the base, and CTBUH standards include this platform in the total height. Taipei 101's records for roof height and highest occupied floor were briefly surpassed by the Shanghai World Financial Center in 2008 but were later overtaken by the Burj Khalifa in 2009. From 26 February to 6 March 2022, the tower's lights displayed blue and yellow in solidarity with Ukraine in response to the Russian invasion. The building's design incorporates a number of features to withstand typhoon winds and earthquakes, including outrigger trusses at eight-floor intervals and a foundation reinforced by 380 piles extending 80 meters into the ground. The structure is one of the most stable ever built, with its facade system and tuned mass damper contributing to lateral rigidity and resistance to seismic and wind forces. The building's height of 508.2 meters (1,667 feet) to its architectural top surpassed the Petronas Towers' height of 451.9 meters (1,483 feet), and it held the title of world's tallest building from 31 March 2004 to 10 March 2010 (six years), and for 12 years housed the fastest elevator at 61 km/h (38 mph). As of 2023, it remains the eleventh-tallest building in the world.

Curled ruyi figures serve as a design motif throughout Taipei 101, with each exterior ruyi ornament standing at least 8 m (26 ft) tall. Though the ruyi shape is traditional, its execution in industrial metal reflects a modern aesthetic. The ruyi is an ancient talisman associated with heavenly clouds and symbolizes healing, protection, and fulfillment, often appearing in celebrations marking new career achievements. The sweeping curved roof of the adjacent mall ends in a large ruyi that provides shade for pedestrians. At night, the tower's bright yellow pinnacle gives it the appearance of a candle or torch, representing liberty and welcome, with its lights displaying one of seven colors from 6 to 10 p.m. on a weekly schedule. From 26 February to 6 March 2022, the colors were changed to blue and yellow in solidarity with Ukraine due to the 2022 Russian invasion. The east-side adjoining structure connects to the symbolism of time, with the circular park functioning as a giant sundial, casting shadows to mark afternoon for building occupants, and a wind-powered clock at the entrance reflecting the building's wind shear. Taipei 101 incorporates feng shui principles, exemplified by a large granite fountain at the intersection of Songlian and Xinyi Roads near the east entrance, where a spinning ball faces the tower; this design counters the potential energy drain at a T-junction and redirects ch'i, a concept in feng shui. Two restaurants operate on the 85th floor: Diamond Tony's, serving European-style seafood and steak, and 85TD, offering Chinese cuisine. The 86th floor is entirely occupied by the high-class buffet restaurant A Joy. The adjacent multistory retail mall hosts hundreds of fashionable stores, restaurants, clubs, and attractions, featuring the curled ruyi motif and observing feng shui traditions. A tenant directory is posted in the lobby, with the 44th floor renamed the 43rd and the 43rd floor becoming 42A to avoid the culturally unlucky number 4. As of 1 January 2011, the highest occupied office floor (excluding the observatory and restaurants) was the 75th, and the building was at least 70% occupied. Floors 92 through 100 are officially designated as communication floors, though no known radio or TV stations broadcast from the top. The indoor/outdoor rooftop observatory on the 101st floor opened to the public on 14 June 2019, initially with a daily quota of 36 visitors. The indoor observatory, located on the 88th and 89th floors at 383.4 m (1,258 ft) above ground, offers 360-degree views, large UV-protected windows, voice tours in eight languages, and informative displays, including the world's largest and heaviest visible damper. It is open 13 hours daily (9:00 am–10:00 pm) and accessible via high-speed elevators from the 5th floor. The outdoor observatories are at 391.8 m (1,285 ft) and 449.2 m (1,474 ft), making them the second-highest observation deck in any skyscraper and the highest in Taiwan. The outdoor observatory is open during the same hours as weather permits and requires safety equipment such as a safety belt. Tickets can be purchased on-site at the mall's 5th floor or online through the observatory's website. On its opening, Taipei 101 won the Emporis Skyscraper Award, placing first. It received a platinum rating from the Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) system, becoming the tallest energy-conservation building globally. In 2017, it was awarded the Asia Responsible Entrepreneurship Award (AREA), and in another recognition, it won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award in the Performance category. The double-deck elevators, manufactured by the Japanese Toshiba Elevator and Building Systems Corporation (TELC), set a world record in 2004 at 60.6 km/h (37.7 mi/h), 16.83 m/s (1,010 m/min), 34.7% faster than the previous record holders in Yokohama, which reached 12.5 m/s (45 km/h, 28 mph). These elevators transport visitors from the fifth to the 89th floor in 37 seconds and feature an aerodynamic body, full pressurization, state-of-the-art emergency braking, and the world's first triple-stage anti-overshooting system, each costing NT$80 million (US$2.4 million). In 2016, the title of world's fastest elevator was taken by the Shanghai Tower, and shortly after, it was passed to the Guangzhou CTF Finance Centre. Artworks in and around the building include Rebecca Horn's Dialog between Yin and Yang (2002), Robert Indiana's 1-0 (2002) and Love (2003), Ariel Moscovici's Between Earth and Sky (2002), Chung Pu's Global Circle (2002), Jill Watson's City Composition (2002), and Kang Mu Hsiang's Infinite Life (2013). The indoor observatory regularly hosts exhibitions featuring artists such as Wu Ching (gold sculpture), Ping-huang Chang (traditional painting), and Po-lin Chi (aerial photography).
